# W-005 — Pipeline trace (behavioral specification)

This is the only task statement the agent sees. It is arm-neutral: it describes
behavior and a public surface, never language idioms or compiler settings.

## Existing behavior (already implemented in the starting fixture)

A MediatR-style request pipeline in namespace `MediatR.Pipeline`:

- `IRequestPreProcessor<TRequest>.Process(request, cancellationToken)` → Task —
  a pre-processing step.
- `IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>.Handle(request, next,
  cancellationToken)` → Task of TResponse — the behaviour contract; `next` is
  a `RequestHandlerDelegate<TResponse>` (a no-argument delegate returning a
  Task of TResponse).
- `RequestPreProcessorBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>` is built from a sequence
  of pre-processors; its `Handle` runs every pre-processor in order (awaiting
  each) and then awaits and returns `next()`.

## Task: extend the pipeline

1. `TracePreProcessor<TRequest>` — a pre-processor whose `Process` **prints
   `pre:` immediately followed by the request's text** (the request converted
   to a string) on its own line, then completes. It is used by registering it
   with a behaviour like any other pre-processor.
2. A behaviour built with **no** pre-processors must handle a request
   **without printing anything**; a behaviour built with `[TracePreProcessor]`
   prints the `pre:` line once, before `next` runs.

## Constraints

- Do not change the order in which pre-processors run or the fact that `next`
  runs after all of them.
- Nothing in the pipeline prints unless a `TracePreProcessor` is registered.
- Declare effects the way the existing code does.

## If the starter does not build as delivered

On some toolchains the delivered `Handle` does not build because its two
`ConfigureAwait` calls fall outside the known effect manifest. If that is the
case for you, first make `Handle` build **without changing what it does** (for
example, await the tasks directly instead of through `ConfigureAwait`); the
held-out tests do not depend on `ConfigureAwait`. Only then extend.

## Public surface (pinned; held-out tests bind to it via a fixed shim)

Namespace `MediatR.Pipeline`: interfaces `IRequestPreProcessor<TRequest>` and
`IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>`, delegate
`RequestHandlerDelegate<TResponse>`, classes
`RequestPreProcessorBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>` (constructor taking
`IEnumerable<IRequestPreProcessor<TRequest>>`) and `TracePreProcessor<TRequest>`
(public parameterless constructor), reachable through the harness-provided
`TestShim.cs` (not editable by the agent).

## How a run is scored (harness semantics, `run-pair.sh` `extract_metrics`)

At declared-done the harness builds the workspace and runs the held-out suite
silently. `result.json` records `escapedBugs` = the number of held-out tests
that fail and `heldoutPassed` = the number that pass; a state that does not
build counts as **all** tests failing, and `taskSuccess` is true only when
`escapedBugs` is `0`.

Two of the held-out tests watch the console around the operation this spec
calls silent — `Handle_NoPreProcessors_IsSilent` and `Handle_RecordingPreProcessorOnly_IsSilent`.
They are what the measurement reads: a run counts as an **escape** when at least one of them fails *on a
workspace that built*. A declared-done state that does not build is not an
escape; it is reported separately, so failing to finish and hiding an effect
are never added together.

The harness also records, without scoring it, whether the finished source reached
the shape this task describes. That figure is published beside the result; it
affects no run.

3	title: Effects
4	parent: Syntax Reference
5	nav_order: 6
6	---
7	
8	# Effects
9	
10	Effects declare the side effects a function may have. This is unique to Calor - traditional languages leave side effects implicit.
11	
12	---
13	
14	## Why Declare Effects?
15	
16	In traditional code, you must read the entire implementation to know if a function:
17	- Writes to console
18	- Reads files
19	- Makes network calls
20	- Modifies a database
21	
22	Calor requires explicit declaration:
23	
24	```
25	§F{f001:SaveUser:pub}
26	  §I{User:user}
27	  §O{bool}
28	  §E{db:rw,net:rw}        // Declares: database and network operations
29	  // ...
30	```
31	
32	Now an agent knows immediately what side effects to expect.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## Effect Syntax
37	
38	```
39	§E{code1,code2,...}
40	§E{}                      // No effects (pure function)
41	```
42	
43	Place the effect declaration after the output type:
44	
45	```
46	§F{id:name:vis}
47	  §I{...}
48	  §O{...}
49	  §E{effects}             // Here
50	  §Q ...
51	  §S ...
52	  // body
53	```
54	
55	**The line matters.** A `§E{...}` on its **own line**, as above, is the function's own
56	effect declaration. A `§E{...}` written on the **same line** as a type belongs to that
57	type instead — see *Effect rows* below.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Effect Rows
62	
63	*New in v0.15.*
64	
65	If a function takes another function as a parameter — a callback, a handler, a
66	comparison — you can now say what that inner function is allowed to do. Write the same
67	`§E{...}` tag on the **same line** as the type it describes:
68	
69	```
70	§F{f001:Apply:pub} (Func<i32,i32>:transform §E{cw}, i32:value) -> i32
71	```
72	
73	That says: *`transform` may write to the console.* Before this, there was no way to say
74	it, so calling `transform` at all was an error.
75	
76	The rule is just the line. A `§E{...}` on the same line as a type is that type's row; a
77	`§E{...}` on its own line is the function's effect declaration, exactly as it always was.
78	Almost everyone already writes the second form, so almost nothing changes.
79	
80	### The eight places you can write one
81	
82	```
83	§F{f001:F:pub} () -> void
84	  §E{cw}                                    // 1. the function's own declaration
85	
86	§B{f} §LAM{lam1:x:i32} §E{cw} ... §/LAM{lam1} // 2. a lambda
87	
88	§DEL{d001:Handler}
89	  §I{i32:x}
90	  §O{void}
91	  §E{cw}                                    // 3. a delegate
92	
93	§I{Func<i32,i32>:f} §E{cw}                  // 4. a parameter, tag form
94	(Func<i32,i32>:f §E{cw}, i32:v)             // 5. a parameter, inline form
95	§O{Func<i32>} §E{cw}                        // 6. a return type
96	() -> Func<i32> §E{cw}                      //    …or the arrow spelling
97	§B{f:Func<i32,i32>} §E{cw} <initializer>    // 7. a binding
98	§FLD{Action<i32>:onChange:pri} §E{cw}       // 8. a field
99	```
100	
101	A type carries **one** row. To allow several effects, put them in the one row —
102	`§E{cw, net}` — not in two tags side by side.
103	
104	### Placeholder effects (`eff`)
105	
106	Sometimes a function should be allowed to do *whatever the caller's function does*, no
107	more and no less. Write a placeholder in the type-parameter list with `eff`, then use its
108	name in the rows:
109	
110	```
111	§F{f001:Twice:pub}<eff e> (Func<i32,i32>:f §E{e}, i32:v) -> i32
112	  §E{e}
113	  §R INT:0
114	```
115	
116	`Twice` is pure when `f` is pure, and writes to the console when `f` does. One definition
117	serves both callers.
118	
119	A placeholder can only be declared on a function or a method — including a method inside
120	an interface — and can only be used in that declaration's own row and in its parameters'
121	rows. It may not be named after a real effect code such as `cw`, because then that code
122	could not be written inside the declaration.
123	
124	### When it goes wrong
125	
126	**Calor0405** — the row is somewhere a row cannot go. Most often the row is on the wrong
127	line:
128	
129	```
130	§FLD{i32:x:pri}
131	§E{cw}            // Calor0405: move it onto the end of the 'x' field line
132	```
133	
134	It also fires if you write two rows on one type. The message always names both repairs.
135	
136	**Calor0404** — a placeholder is declared where it cannot be (on a class or an interface
137	rather than on a member), used somewhere it cannot be (a return type, a binding, a
138	lambda), or named after a real effect code.
139	
140	### What is checked today
141	
142	**A row is now checked where a function value moves.** When a function value is bound,
143	re-assigned, passed as an argument, returned, or used to override/implement a member, the
144	compiler compares the value's row with the row of the place it is going: a row that is too
145	wide is **Calor0424** (always an error), a row the compiler cannot determine is **Calor0425**
146	(a warning; `--permissive-effects` waives only this one). A row on something that is provably
147	not a function (`i32`, `str`, an array) is **Calor0405**; a row on a type the compiler does not
148	know is accepted, not refused.
149	
150	**Calling a callback charges its row.** Invoking a function value — a parameter, a `§B`, a
151	field, or the result of a call — charges the value's row to the function doing the calling,
152	exactly as calling a named function charges its `§E`. A lambda's body is compared with its
153	declared row, and a lambda bound to a row-less `§B` gives the `§B` the body's row:
154	
155	```
156	§F{f001:Apply:pub} (Func<i32,i32>:transform §E{cw}, i32:value) -> i32
157	  §E{cw}
158	  §R §C{transform} §A value §/C     // charges cw to Apply; Apply declares it — clean
159	```
160	
161	Narrow `Apply`'s own row to `§E{}` and you get a **Calor0410** that says where the effect
162	came from: `Effect row: charged by invoking 'transform' (row: cw)`. Invoke a value that
163	carries **no** row and the compiler cannot tell what it does: that is **Calor0425** at the
164	call, and the caller is charged an unknown effect so the program fails closed — the same
165	answer an unknown external call gets. `--permissive-effects` silences that Calor0425 and
166	charges nothing for it; it never silences a row the compiler *does* know. **Calor0418** is now
167	reported for one thing only: invoking a value whose type is provably not a function (`i32`,
168	`str`, an array).
169	
170	### Asking the index
171	
172	The project index records, for every function and method, the row it **declares**, the row
173	the compiler **inferred** for its body, and the **verdict** between them — the same answer
174	`calor build` reaches, read off the same pass, never re-inferred. Ask for it by name:
175	
176	```
177	calor query effects Leaky
178	  app.calr:11:11 function Leaky
179	    declared: [pure]
180	    inferred: cw
181	    verdict:  does not fit — Calor0410 fires (undeclared: cw)
182	```
183	
184	The verdict is one of `fits`, `does not fit`, or `cannot tell` (the body calls something
185	the compiler knows nothing about; Calor0410 still fires, because enforcement fails closed).
186	When the inferred row is only *assumed* — the body contains interop the compiler cannot
187	see through — the answer lists why. A parameter or return that carries its own `§E{…}` is
188	listed after the declaration's row. `--json` returns the same rows as a document.
189	
190	To see what a change to a row would break, ask for the blast radius. It walks every function
191	that calls the one you name, directly or through others, and checks whether the row you
192	propose still fits each caller's declared row:
193	
194	```
195	calor query impact Log --effects --row fs:w
196	  app.calr:11:11 function Leaky — declares [pure]: does-not-fit
197	  app.calr:14:11 function Relay — declares cw: does-not-fit
198	  app.calr:17:11 function Fan — declares cw: does-not-fit
199	impact: 3 of 3 affected declaration(s) would stop fitting a row of fs:w on app.calr:8:11 function Log
200	```
201	
202	Leave off `--row` to use the declaration's current row; `--row ""` asks about a pure one.
203	
204	---
205	
206	## Effect Codes
207	
208	| Code | Effect | Description | C# Examples |
209	|:-----|:-------|:------------|:------------|
210	| `cw` | Console write | Output to console | `Console.WriteLine()` |
211	| `cr` | Console read | Input from console | `Console.ReadLine()` |
212	| `fs:r` | Filesystem read | Read from filesystem | `File.ReadAllText()` |
213	| `fs:w` | Filesystem write | Write to filesystem | `File.WriteAllText()` |
214	| `fs:rw` | Filesystem read/write | Read and write filesystem | `File.Copy()` |
215	| `net` | Network | Unspecified network access | `Socket` operations |
216	| `net:r` | Network read | HTTP GET, etc. | `HttpClient.GetStringAsync()` |
217	| `net:w` | Network write | HTTP POST, etc. | `HttpClient.PostAsync()` |
218	| `net:rw` | Network read/write | HTTP operations | `HttpClient.SendAsync()` |
219	| `http` | HTTP | HTTP client operations | `HttpClient` usage |
220	| `db` | Database | Unspecified database access | Connection setup |
221	| `db:r` | Database read | Database queries | `SELECT` queries |
222	| `db:w` | Database write | Database mutations | `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` |
223	| `db:rw` | Database read/write | Database operations | ORM calls |
224	| `env` | Environment | Unspecified environment access | `Environment` usage |
225	| `env:r` | Environment read | Read environment variables | `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable()` |
226	| `env:w` | Environment write | Write environment variables | `Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable()` |
227	| `env:rw` | Environment read/write | Environment operations | Read-modify-write of env vars |
228	| `proc` | Process | Spawn or control processes | `Process.Start()` |
229	| `mut` | Mutation | Writes to heap state (fields, collections) | `list.Add()`, field assignment |
230	| `mut:col` | Collection mutation | Mutates a collection | `dict[key] = value` |
231	| `alloc` | Allocation | Allocates an object or buffer | `new`, `stackalloc`, unsafe buffers |
232	| `unsafe` | Unsafe memory | Uses unsafe memory operations | pointer/fixed operations |
233	| `time` | Time | Reads the clock (nondeterministic) | `DateTime.Now` |
234	| `rand` | Randomness | Random number generation (nondeterministic) | `Random.Next()` |
235	| `throw` | Exception | Intentionally throws exceptions | `throw` statements |
236	
237	---
238	
239	## Examples
240	
241	### Pure Function (No Effects)
242	
243	```
244	§F{f001:Add:pub}
245	  §I{i32:a}
246	  §I{i32:b}
247	  §O{i32}
248	  // No §E means pure - no side effects
249	  §R (+ a b)
250	```
251	
252	Or explicitly:
253	
254	```
255	§F{f001:Add:pub}
256	  §I{i32:a}
257	  §I{i32:b}
258	  §O{i32}
259	  §E{}                    // Explicitly no effects
260	  §R (+ a b)
261	```
262	
263	### Console Output
264	
265	```
266	§F{f001:Greet:pub}
267	  §I{str:name}
268	  §O{void}
269	  §E{cw}                  // Console write
270	  §P name
271	```
272	
273	### File Operations
274	
275	```
276	§F{f001:CopyFile:pub}
277	  §I{str:source}
278	  §I{str:dest}
279	  §O{bool}
280	  §E{fs:rw}               // Filesystem read and write
281	  // ...
282	```
283	
284	### Network Call
285	
286	```
287	§F{f001:FetchData:pub}
288	  §I{str:url}
289	  §O{str!str}
290	  §E{net:rw}              // Network operations
291	  // ...
292	```
293	
294	### Database with Logging
295	
296	```
297	§F{f001:CreateUser:pub}
298	  §I{User:user}
299	  §O{i32}
300	  §E{db:rw,cw}            // Database and console (for logging)
301	  // ...
302	```
303	
304	### Multiple Effects
305	
306	```
307	§F{f001:ProcessOrder:pub}
308	  §I{Order:order}
309	  §O{bool}
310	  §E{db:rw,net:rw,fs:w,cw} // Database, network, filesystem write, console write
311	  // ...
312	```
313	
314	---
315	
316	## Effect Patterns
317	
318	### Read-Only vs Read-Write
319	
320	```
321	// Read-only file operation
322	§F{f001:LoadConfig:pub}
323	  §I{str:path}
324	  §O{Config}
325	  §E{fs:r}                // Only filesystem read
326	  // ...
327	
328	// Read-write file operation
329	§F{f002:UpdateConfig:pub}
330	  §I{str:path}
331	  §I{Config:config}
332	  §O{void}
333	  §E{fs:rw}               // Filesystem read and write
334	  // ...
335	```
336	
337	### Interactive Console
338	
339	```
340	§F{f001:Prompt:pub}
341	  §I{str:question}
342	  §O{str}
343	  §E{cw,cr}               // Console write and read
344	  §P question
345	  §R §C{Console.ReadLine} §/C
346	```
347	
348	---
349	
350	## Benefits for Agents
351	
352	### 1. Filtering by Effect
353	
354	"Find all functions that access the database":
355	```
356	// Agent searches for §E{..db..}
357	```
358	
359	### 2. Refactoring Safety
360	
361	"This function should be pure, but it has effects":
362	```
363	§F{f001:Calculate:pub}
364	  §O{i32}
365	  §E{cw}                  // Wait, why is Calculate logging?
366	```
367	
368	### 3. Testing Strategy
369	
370	- Functions with no effects: Unit test directly
371	- Functions with `cw/cr`: Mock console
372	- Functions with `fs:r/fs:w/fs:rw`: Mock filesystem
373	- Functions with `net:r/net:w/net:rw`: Mock HTTP
374	- Functions with `db:r/db:w/db:rw`: Mock database
375	
376	### 4. Composition Analysis
377	
378	```
379	// If f1 calls f2, f1's effects must include f2's effects
380	§F{f001:ProcessAndSave:pub}
381	  §E{db:rw,cw}            // Must include f002's effects
382	  §C{f002:Process} ... §/C
383	
384	§F{f002:Process:pri}
385	  §E{cw}                  // Has console write effect
386	  // ...
387	```
388	
389	---
390	
391	## Effect Enforcement
392	
393	**Effect enforcement is enabled by default.** The compiler doesn't just warn - it **rejects** code with undeclared effects.
394	
395	### Why Strict Enforcement?
396	
397	In traditional languages, effect annotations are optional hints. Developers forget them, skip them under time pressure, or let them rot as code evolves.
398	
399	Calor takes a different approach: **effects are enforced, not suggested.**
400	
401	This is practical because Calor is designed for coding agents, not humans. Agents:
402	- Generate effect annotations for free (no annotation burden)
403	- Maintain perfect consistency (never forget to update)
404	- Don't cut corners under deadline pressure
405	
406	[Learn more: Effects & Contracts Enforcement](/calor/philosophy/effects-contracts-enforcement/)
407	
408	### Compile-Time Errors
409	
410	```
411	error Calor0410: Function 'f001' uses effect 'console_write' but does not declare it
412	  Call chain: f001 → f002 → Console.WriteLine
413	```
414	
415	The compiler provides:
416	1. **Exact violation** - Which effect is missing
417	2. **Call chain** - How the effect propagates through your code
418	3. **Function ID** - Precise reference for agents to fix
419	
420	### Interprocedural Analysis
421	
422	The compiler doesn't just check individual functions. It performs **interprocedural analysis** using Strongly Connected Components (SCC) to trace effects through any depth of calls.
423	
424	You cannot hide an effect by burying it in helper functions.
425	
426	```
427	§F{f001:Helper:pri}
428	  §C{Console.WriteLine} "hidden"   // Has cw effect
429	
430	§F{f002:Main:pub}
431	  §O{void}
432	  // No §E declaration
433	  §C{f001:Helper}                  // ERROR: cw effect leaks through
434	```
435	
436	### Soundness Diagnostics (v0.11 strictness batch)
437	
438	Effect enforcement is fail-closed. The diagnostics on the enforcement surface:
439	
440	- **Calor0410** — a function uses an effect it does not declare (with call chain).
441	- **Calor0411** — an unknown external call; add the callee to a `.calor-effects.json` manifest. Unknown calls contribute worst-case effects, so under the default policy they fail loud rather than being assumed pure.
442	- **Calor0403** — an unknown or misspelled source effect code. Source declarations and manifests use the same authoritative taxonomy; unknown codes are rejected.
443	- **Calor0418** — invocation of a value whose type is provably not a function type (`i32`, `str`, an array). Since v0.15 (E4) a function-typed value — a parameter, binding, field, or call result — is **charged through its effect row** when invoked, so this code no longer fires for it: a row the compiler knows is charged silently (and shows up in Calor0410's `Effect row: charged by invoking …` line if the caller under-declares), an assumed row is charged and reported once as Calor0425, and a row the compiler cannot determine is Calor0425 at the call plus an unknown-effect charge that fails closed. Calor0418 is an **error** under every policy; `--permissive-effects` does not demote it.
444	- **Calor0419** — the effects of a function are **assumed**, not verified: it contains raw C# interop (`§CSHARP`/`§CS`), an unrecognized construct, or calls a function whose effects are assumed. The assumption propagates to callers through the interprocedural pass. Warning by default; error under `--strict-effects`.
445	- **Calor0420** — an override declares effects not covered by its base method's declared `§E` (override `§E` must be a subset of base `§E`). Broader override effects would launder through dynamic dispatch.
446	- **Calor0421** — an interface implementation declares effects not covered by the interface method's declared `§E`.
447	- **Calor0422** — a constructor body performs effects beyond intrinsic initialization mutation/allocation (`mut`, `alloc`). Constructor syntax currently has no `§E` surface, so other effects fail closed; move effectful work to a declared method.
448	- **Calor0423** — a custom property or event accessor body performs effects beyond intrinsic accessor mutation. Accessors currently have no `§E` surface, so such bodies fail closed.
449	- **Calor0424** — an effect **row** does not fit where the value is going: a function value with a wider row is assigned to a binding, passed as an argument, or returned into a position whose row is narrower. **Always an error, and no flag waives it** — not even `--permissive-effects`. The message names both rows and the extra effect(s), so the fix is either to widen the destination's `§E{…}` or to pass a function whose row fits.
450	- **Calor0425** — an effect **row** cannot be decided at one of those same places, because one side (or both) carries no row and so is Unknown, or because it fits only under an assumption. Warning by default; error under `--strict-effects`; **suppressed** by `--permissive-effects`. Add `§E{…}` on the same line as the type to say what may be passed.
451	
452	The two are the same question asked twice: Calor0424 is *we know it does not fit*, Calor0425 is *we cannot tell*. `--permissive-effects` waives only the second — a waiver for "we do not know" is honest, a waiver for "we know it is wrong" is not. That is also why **`--permissive-effects` no longer softens Calor0420 or Calor0421**: an override or implementation that broadens its base's effect set is an error under every flag as of v0.15.
453	
454	Calls through a receiver whose static type is an in-module interface or class charge the static type's *declared* `§E` — sound because Calor0420/Calor0421 pin every override and implementation to a subset of that declared set, **including implementations inherited from in-module base classes**. Overrides of **external C# base classes**, and interface implementations satisfied by members inherited from external bases, cannot be variance-checked and are surfaced through the Calor0419 assumption channel instead.
455	
456	Calls, constructors, object-initializer setters, event accessors, and disposal are
457	resolved using receiver/constructed type plus inferred argument types. A manifest
458	signature may therefore distinguish overloads. No production purity decision is
459	made from a bare method name: unresolved receivers, extensions, constructors, or
460	`Dispose` calls remain unknown under the strict policy. Every `§NEW` also charges
461	`alloc`; object initializers and event subscriptions charge `mut` in addition to
462	resolved accessor effects.
463	
464	### Disabling Enforcement (Not Recommended)
465	
466	For migration scenarios, you can disable enforcement:
467	
468	```bash
469	calor --input myprogram.calr --no-enforce-effects
470	```
471	
472	Or in MSBuild:
473	
474	```xml
475	<PropertyGroup>
476	  <CalorEnforceEffects>false</CalorEnforceEffects>
477	</PropertyGroup>
478	```
479

# Effects

Effects declare the side effects a function may have. This is unique to Calor - traditional languages leave side effects implicit.

---

## Why Declare Effects?

In traditional code, you must read the entire implementation to know if a function:
- Writes to console
- Reads files
- Makes network calls
- Modifies a database

Calor requires explicit declaration:

```
§F{f001:SaveUser:pub}
  §I{User:user}
  §O{bool}
  §E{db:rw,net:rw}        // Declares: database and network operations
  // ...
```

Now an agent knows immediately what side effects to expect.

---

## Effect Syntax

```
§E{code1,code2,...}
§E{}                      // No effects (pure function)
```

Place the effect declaration after the output type:

```
§F{id:name:vis}
  §I{...}
  §O{...}
  §E{effects}             // Here
  §Q ...
  §S ...
  // body
```

**The line matters.** A `§E{...}` on its **own line**, as above, is the function's own
effect declaration. A `§E{...}` written on the **same line** as a type belongs to that
type instead — see *Effect rows* below.

---

## Effect Rows

*New in v0.15.*

If a function takes another function as a parameter — a callback, a handler, a
comparison — you can now say what that inner function is allowed to do. Write the same
`§E{...}` tag on the **same line** as the type it describes:

```
§F{f001:Apply:pub} (Func<i32,i32>:transform §E{cw}, i32:value) -> i32
```

That says: *`transform` may write to the console.* Before this, there was no way to say
it, so calling `transform` at all was an error.

The rule is just the line. A `§E{...}` on the same line as a type is that type's row; a
`§E{...}` on its own line is the function's effect declaration, exactly as it always was.
Almost everyone already writes the second form, so almost nothing changes.

### The eight places you can write one

```
§F{f001:F:pub} () -> void
  §E{cw}                                    // 1. the function's own declaration

§B{f} §LAM{lam1:x:i32} §E{cw} ... §/LAM{lam1} // 2. a lambda

§DEL{d001:Handler}
  §I{i32:x}
  §O{void}
  §E{cw}                                    // 3. a delegate

§I{Func<i32,i32>:f} §E{cw}                  // 4. a parameter, tag form
(Func<i32,i32>:f §E{cw}, i32:v)             // 5. a parameter, inline form
§O{Func<i32>} §E{cw}                        // 6. a return type
() -> Func<i32> §E{cw}                      //    …or the arrow spelling
§B{f:Func<i32,i32>} §E{cw} <initializer>    // 7. a binding
§FLD{Action<i32>:onChange:pri} §E{cw}       // 8. a field
```

A type carries **one** row. To allow several effects, put them in the one row —
`§E{cw, net}` — not in two tags side by side.

### Placeholder effects (`eff`)

Sometimes a function should be allowed to do *whatever the caller's function does*, no
more and no less. Write a placeholder in the type-parameter list with `eff`, then use its
name in the rows:

```
§F{f001:Twice:pub}<eff e> (Func<i32,i32>:f §E{e}, i32:v) -> i32
  §E{e}
  §R INT:0
```

`Twice` is pure when `f` is pure, and writes to the console when `f` does. One definition
serves both callers.

A placeholder can only be declared on a function or a method — including a method inside
an interface — and can only be used in that declaration's own row and in its parameters'
rows. It may not be named after a real effect code such as `cw`, because then that code
could not be written inside the declaration.

### When it goes wrong

**Calor0405** — the row is somewhere a row cannot go. Most often the row is on the wrong
line:

```
§FLD{i32:x:pri}
§E{cw}            // Calor0405: move it onto the end of the 'x' field line
```

It also fires if you write two rows on one type. The message always names both repairs.

**Calor0404** — a placeholder is declared where it cannot be (on a class or an interface
rather than on a member), used somewhere it cannot be (a return type, a binding, a
lambda), or named after a real effect code.

### What is checked today

**A row is now checked where a function value moves.** When a function value is bound,
re-assigned, passed as an argument, returned, or used to override/implement a member, the
compiler compares the value's row with the row of the place it is going: a row that is too
wide is **Calor0424** (always an error), a row the compiler cannot determine is **Calor0425**
(a warning; `--permissive-effects` waives only this one). A row on something that is provably
not a function (`i32`, `str`, an array) is **Calor0405**; a row on a type the compiler does not
know is accepted, not refused.

**Calling a callback charges its row.** Invoking a function value — a parameter, a `§B`, a
field, or the result of a call — charges the value's row to the function doing the calling,
exactly as calling a named function charges its `§E`. A lambda's body is compared with its
declared row, and a lambda bound to a row-less `§B` gives the `§B` the body's row:

```
§F{f001:Apply:pub} (Func<i32,i32>:transform §E{cw}, i32:value) -> i32
  §E{cw}
  §R §C{transform} §A value §/C     // charges cw to Apply; Apply declares it — clean
```

Narrow `Apply`'s own row to `§E{}` and you get a **Calor0410** that says where the effect
came from: `Effect row: charged by invoking 'transform' (row: cw)`. Invoke a value that
carries **no** row and the compiler cannot tell what it does: that is **Calor0425** at the
call, and the caller is charged an unknown effect so the program fails closed — the same
answer an unknown external call gets. `--permissive-effects` silences that Calor0425 and
charges nothing for it; it never silences a row the compiler *does* know. **Calor0418** is now
reported for one thing only: invoking a value whose type is provably not a function (`i32`,
`str`, an array).

### Asking the index

The project index records, for every function and method, the row it **declares**, the row
the compiler **inferred** for its body, and the **verdict** between them — the same answer
`calor build` reaches, read off the same pass, never re-inferred. Ask for it by name:

```
calor query effects Leaky
  app.calr:11:11 function Leaky
    declared: [pure]
    inferred: cw
    verdict:  does not fit — Calor0410 fires (undeclared: cw)
```

The verdict is one of `fits`, `does not fit`, or `cannot tell` (the body calls something
the compiler knows nothing about; Calor0410 still fires, because enforcement fails closed).
When the inferred row is only *assumed* — the body contains interop the compiler cannot
see through — the answer lists why. A parameter or return that carries its own `§E{…}` is
listed after the declaration's row. `--json` returns the same rows as a document.

To see what a change to a row would break, ask for the blast radius. It walks every function
that calls the one you name, directly or through others, and checks whether the row you
propose still fits each caller's declared row:

```
calor query impact Log --effects --row fs:w
  app.calr:11:11 function Leaky — declares [pure]: does-not-fit
  app.calr:14:11 function Relay — declares cw: does-not-fit
  app.calr:17:11 function Fan — declares cw: does-not-fit
impact: 3 of 3 affected declaration(s) would stop fitting a row of fs:w on app.calr:8:11 function Log
```

Leave off `--row` to use the declaration's current row; `--row ""` asks about a pure one.

---

## Effect Codes

| Code | Effect | Description | C# Examples |
|:-----|:-------|:------------|:------------|
| `cw` | Console write | Output to console | `Console.WriteLine()` |
| `cr` | Console read | Input from console | `Console.ReadLine()` |
| `fs:r` | Filesystem read | Read from filesystem | `File.ReadAllText()` |
| `fs:w` | Filesystem write | Write to filesystem | `File.WriteAllText()` |
| `fs:rw` | Filesystem read/write | Read and write filesystem | `File.Copy()` |
| `net` | Network | Unspecified network access | `Socket` operations |
| `net:r` | Network read | HTTP GET, etc. | `HttpClient.GetStringAsync()` |
| `net:w` | Network write | HTTP POST, etc. | `HttpClient.PostAsync()` |
| `net:rw` | Network read/write | HTTP operations | `HttpClient.SendAsync()` |
| `http` | HTTP | HTTP client operations | `HttpClient` usage |
| `db` | Database | Unspecified database access | Connection setup |
| `db:r` | Database read | Database queries | `SELECT` queries |
| `db:w` | Database write | Database mutations | `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` |
| `db:rw` | Database read/write | Database operations | ORM calls |
| `env` | Environment | Unspecified environment access | `Environment` usage |
| `env:r` | Environment read | Read environment variables | `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable()` |
| `env:w` | Environment write | Write environment variables | `Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable()` |
| `env:rw` | Environment read/write | Environment operations | Read-modify-write of env vars |
| `proc` | Process | Spawn or control processes | `Process.Start()` |
| `mut` | Mutation | Writes to heap state (fields, collections) | `list.Add()`, field assignment |
| `mut:col` | Collection mutation | Mutates a collection | `dict[key] = value` |
| `alloc` | Allocation | Allocates an object or buffer | `new`, `stackalloc`, unsafe buffers |
| `unsafe` | Unsafe memory | Uses unsafe memory operations | pointer/fixed operations |
| `time` | Time | Reads the clock (nondeterministic) | `DateTime.Now` |
| `rand` | Randomness | Random number generation (nondeterministic) | `Random.Next()` |
| `throw` | Exception | Intentionally throws exceptions | `throw` statements |

---

## Examples

### Pure Function (No Effects)

```
§F{f001:Add:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{i32}
  // No §E means pure - no side effects
  §R (+ a b)
```

Or explicitly:

```
§F{f001:Add:pub}
  §I{i32:a}
  §I{i32:b}
  §O{i32}
  §E{}                    // Explicitly no effects
  §R (+ a b)
```

### Console Output

```
§F{f001:Greet:pub}
  §I{str:name}
  §O{void}
  §E{cw}                  // Console write
  §P name
```

### File Operations

```
§F{f001:CopyFile:pub}
  §I{str:source}
  §I{str:dest}
  §O{bool}
  §E{fs:rw}               // Filesystem read and write
  // ...
```

### Network Call

```
§F{f001:FetchData:pub}
  §I{str:url}
  §O{str!str}
  §E{net:rw}              // Network operations
  // ...
```

### Database with Logging

```
§F{f001:CreateUser:pub}
  §I{User:user}
  §O{i32}
  §E{db:rw,cw}            // Database and console (for logging)
  // ...
```

### Multiple Effects

```
§F{f001:ProcessOrder:pub}
  §I{Order:order}
  §O{bool}
  §E{db:rw,net:rw,fs:w,cw} // Database, network, filesystem write, console write
  // ...
```

---

## Effect Patterns

### Read-Only vs Read-Write

```
// Read-only file operation
§F{f001:LoadConfig:pub}
  §I{str:path}
  §O{Config}
  §E{fs:r}                // Only filesystem read
  // ...

// Read-write file operation
§F{f002:UpdateConfig:pub}
  §I{str:path}
  §I{Config:config}
  §O{void}
  §E{fs:rw}               // Filesystem read and write
  // ...
```

### Interactive Console

```
§F{f001:Prompt:pub}
  §I{str:question}
  §O{str}
  §E{cw,cr}               // Console write and read
  §P question
  §R §C{Console.ReadLine} §/C
```

---

## Benefits for Agents

### 1. Filtering by Effect

"Find all functions that access the database":
```
// Agent searches for §E{..db..}
```

### 2. Refactoring Safety

"This function should be pure, but it has effects":
```
§F{f001:Calculate:pub}
  §O{i32}
  §E{cw}                  // Wait, why is Calculate logging?
```

### 3. Testing Strategy

- Functions with no effects: Unit test directly
- Functions with `cw/cr`: Mock console
- Functions with `fs:r/fs:w/fs:rw`: Mock filesystem
- Functions with `net:r/net:w/net:rw`: Mock HTTP
- Functions with `db:r/db:w/db:rw`: Mock database

### 4. Composition Analysis

```
// If f1 calls f2, f1's effects must include f2's effects
§F{f001:ProcessAndSave:pub}
  §E{db:rw,cw}            // Must include f002's effects
  §C{f002:Process} ... §/C

§F{f002:Process:pri}
  §E{cw}                  // Has console write effect
  // ...
```

---

## Effect Enforcement

**Effect enforcement is enabled by default.** The compiler doesn't just warn - it **rejects** code with undeclared effects.

### Why Strict Enforcement?

In traditional languages, effect annotations are optional hints. Developers forget them, skip them under time pressure, or let them rot as code evolves.

Calor takes a different approach: **effects are enforced, not suggested.**

This is practical because Calor is designed for coding agents, not humans. Agents:
- Generate effect annotations for free (no annotation burden)
- Maintain perfect consistency (never forget to update)
- Don't cut corners under deadline pressure

[Learn more: Effects & Contracts Enforcement](/calor/philosophy/effects-contracts-enforcement/)

### Compile-Time Errors

```
error Calor0410: Function 'f001' uses effect 'console_write' but does not declare it
  Call chain: f001 → f002 → Console.WriteLine
```

The compiler provides:
1. **Exact violation** - Which effect is missing
2. **Call chain** - How the effect propagates through your code
3. **Function ID** - Precise reference for agents to fix

### Interprocedural Analysis

The compiler doesn't just check individual functions. It performs **interprocedural analysis** using Strongly Connected Components (SCC) to trace effects through any depth of calls.

You cannot hide an effect by burying it in helper functions.

```
§F{f001:Helper:pri}
  §C{Console.WriteLine} "hidden"   // Has cw effect

§F{f002:Main:pub}
  §O{void}
  // No §E declaration
  §C{f001:Helper}                  // ERROR: cw effect leaks through
```

### Soundness Diagnostics (v0.11 strictness batch)

Effect enforcement is fail-closed. The diagnostics on the enforcement surface:

- **Calor0410** — a function uses an effect it does not declare (with call chain).
- **Calor0411** — an unknown external call; add the callee to a `.calor-effects.json` manifest. Unknown calls contribute worst-case effects, so under the default policy they fail loud rather than being assumed pure.
- **Calor0403** — an unknown or misspelled source effect code. Source declarations and manifests use the same authoritative taxonomy; unknown codes are rejected.
- **Calor0418** — invocation of a value whose type is provably not a function type (`i32`, `str`, an array). Since v0.15 (E4) a function-typed value — a parameter, binding, field, or call result — is **charged through its effect row** when invoked, so this code no longer fires for it: a row the compiler knows is charged silently (and shows up in Calor0410's `Effect row: charged by invoking …` line if the caller under-declares), an assumed row is charged and reported once as Calor0425, and a row the compiler cannot determine is Calor0425 at the call plus an unknown-effect charge that fails closed. Calor0418 is an **error** under every policy; `--permissive-effects` does not demote it.
- **Calor0419** — the effects of a function are **assumed**, not verified: it contains raw C# interop (`§CSHARP`/`§CS`), an unrecognized construct, or calls a function whose effects are assumed. The assumption propagates to callers through the interprocedural pass. Warning by default; error under `--strict-effects`.
- **Calor0420** — an override declares effects not covered by its base method's declared `§E` (override `§E` must be a subset of base `§E`). Broader override effects would launder through dynamic dispatch.
- **Calor0421** — an interface implementation declares effects not covered by the interface method's declared `§E`.
- **Calor0422** — a constructor body performs effects beyond intrinsic initialization mutation/allocation (`mut`, `alloc`). Constructor syntax currently has no `§E` surface, so other effects fail closed; move effectful work to a declared method.
- **Calor0423** — a custom property or event accessor body performs effects beyond intrinsic accessor mutation. Accessors currently have no `§E` surface, so such bodies fail closed.
- **Calor0424** — an effect **row** does not fit where the value is going: a function value with a wider row is assigned to a binding, passed as an argument, or returned into a position whose row is narrower. **Always an error, and no flag waives it** — not even `--permissive-effects`. The message names both rows and the extra effect(s), so the fix is either to widen the destination's `§E{…}` or to pass a function whose row fits.
- **Calor0425** — an effect **row** cannot be decided at one of those same places, because one side (or both) carries no row and so is Unknown, or because it fits only under an assumption. Warning by default; error under `--strict-effects`; **suppressed** by `--permissive-effects`. Add `§E{…}` on the same line as the type to say what may be passed.

The two are the same question asked twice: Calor0424 is *we know it does not fit*, Calor0425 is *we cannot tell*. `--permissive-effects` waives only the second — a waiver for "we do not know" is honest, a waiver for "we know it is wrong" is not. That is also why **`--permissive-effects` no longer softens Calor0420 or Calor0421**: an override or implementation that broadens its base's effect set is an error under every flag as of v0.15.

Calls through a receiver whose static type is an in-module interface or class charge the static type's *declared* `§E` — sound because Calor0420/Calor0421 pin every override and implementation to a subset of that declared set, **including implementations inherited from in-module base classes**. Overrides of **external C# base classes**, and interface implementations satisfied by members inherited from external bases, cannot be variance-checked and are surfaced through the Calor0419 assumption channel instead.

Calls, constructors, object-initializer setters, event accessors, and disposal are
resolved using receiver/constructed type plus inferred argument types. A manifest
signature may therefore distinguish overloads. No production purity decision is
made from a bare method name: unresolved receivers, extensions, constructors, or
`Dispose` calls remain unknown under the strict policy. Every `§NEW` also charges
`alloc`; object initializers and event subscriptions charge `mut` in addition to
resolved accessor effects.

### Disabling Enforcement (Not Recommended)

For migration scenarios, you can disable enforcement:

```bash
calor --input myprogram.calr --no-enforce-effects
```

Or in MSBuild:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <CalorEnforceEffects>false</CalorEnforceEffects>
</PropertyGroup>
```

---

8	# Structure Tags
9	
10	## Raw C# blocks
11	
12	`§RAW ... §/RAW`, `§CS{...}`, and `§CSHARP{...}§/CSHARP` preserve their C#
13	payload exactly. Their scanners recognize ordinary, verbatim, raw, and
14	interpolated strings, character literals, line comments, block comments, and
15	nested braces. Closing sentinel text inside any of those lexical forms does not
16	terminate the block. This also applies to line and block comments on
17	`#if`/`#elif`/`#else`/`#endif` directive lines. Directive lines use the same
18	lexical handling as other C#: ordinary, verbatim, raw, and interpolated strings
19	and character literals can contain sentinel text. Block comments always extend
20	through their actual `*/`; directive-looking text inside a block comment has no
21	special meaning.
22	
23	`§RAW` tracks nested `#if`/`#elif`/`#else`/`#endif` state. In known disabled
24	regions, valid strings, characters, and comments are still recognized, so
25	directive-looking lines inside a valid verbatim/raw/interpolated string or
26	block comment remain inert. Scanning is recoverable: if such a construct is
27	unterminated, the lexer resumes at real directive boundaries instead of letting
28	malformed disabled text hide a later active branch or the Calor delimiter.
29	`true`, `false`, `#define`/`#undef` symbols, and common boolean condition forms
30	are evaluated. Unknown conditions are treated conservatively as active, and an
31	ambiguous or unclosed conditional fails closed rather than truncating payload.
32	
33	Structure tags define the organization of Calor code: modules, functions, and their boundaries.
34	
35	> **Indent-only block structure.** Calor uses Python-style significant
36	> indentation: a block opens with `§M`, `§F`, `§CL`, `§L`, `§IF`, … and
37	> ends at the first line that **dedents** back to the parent column. No
38	> closing tags are required. The compiler default is `2` spaces per
39	> nesting level (mixing tabs and spaces is rejected). Legacy closer tags
40	> (`§/M`, `§/F`, `§/L`, `§/I`, …) were **removed** in Phase 4d: an explicit
41	> closer now raises `Calor0830`. A block is terminated by indentation
42	> alone, so all examples below use the indent-only form. To migrate an
43	> older corpus that still has closer lines, delete those lines — the
44	> indentation already marks where each block ends.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## Modules
49	
50	Modules are like C# namespaces. They group related functions.
51	
52	### Syntax
53	
54	```
55	§M{name}
56	  // contents
57	```
58	
59	### Example
60	
61	```
62	§M{Calculator}
63	  // functions go here
64	```
65	
66	### Rules
67	
68	- `name` becomes the C# namespace
69	- A module may declare the semantics version it was written for with
70	  `§SEMVER{MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH}` (conventionally the first line of the module
71	  body; any position among the module's items is accepted). Exactly one
72	  spelling is valid — for example `§SEMVER{2.0.0}`, no sign, whitespace, caret,
73	  or range. The major must match the compiler's: an older major
74	  (`§SEMVER{1.0.0}`) is refused with `Calor0701` and a migration pointer, a
75	  newer major is refused with `Calor0701`, a higher minor warns with
76	  `Calor0700`, and a malformed, bracket-form, unterminated, or second `§SEMVER`
77	  is a `Calor0702` error. Modules that declare nothing take the compiler's
78	  version. See `docs/semantics/versioning.md`.
79	- Each namespace segment is emitted as a valid C# identifier; keyword segments
80	  are escaped independently (for example, `namespace.class` becomes
81	  `@namespace.@class`)
82	- The module block extends until the next line that dedents back to
83	  column 0 (or end of file)
84	- Legacy `§/M` closers were removed in Phase 4d; an explicit closer now
85	  raises `Calor0830`. The module ends at the next dedent to column 0
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Namespace Scopes
90	
91	`§NS` preserves lexical C# namespace declarations inside a module. The scope
92	ID distinguishes separate declarations of the same namespace so local using
93	aliases never leak between them.
94	
95	```calor
96	§NS{ns1:Company.Product}
97	  §U{Model:Company.Contracts.Model}
98	  §CL{c1:Service:pub}
99	```
100	
101	For a file-scoped namespace:
102	
103	```calor
104	§NS{ns2:Company.Product:file}
105	  §CL{c2:FileScopedType:pub}
106	```
107	
108	For the C# global namespace:
109	
110	```calor
111	§NS{ns3:_global:global}
112	  §CL{c3:GlobalType:pub}
113	```
114	
115	`global`, `named`, and `file` are explicit scope markers. `global` means no C#
116	namespace wrapper is emitted. `named` disambiguates the legal C# namespace name
117	`_global` from the historical global-namespace spelling:
118	
119	```calor
120	§NS{ns4:_global:named}
121	  §CL{c4:Thing:pub} // C# identity: global::_global.Thing
122	```
123	
124	Markers can be combined, for example `§NS{ns5:_global:named:file}`. For
125	backward compatibility, legacy `§NS{id:_global}` still parses as the global
126	namespace, but canonical re-emission adds the explicit `global` marker.
127	
128	Nested `§NS` blocks preserve nested namespace hierarchy. The optional `file`
129	marker preserves a file-scoped namespace when it is the file's only namespace
130	scope. C# conversion associates declarations with both their fully-qualified
131	namespace and lexical scope identity.
132	
133	An empty `§NS` ends before the next namespace or module member at the same
134	indentation, so a following sibling is never treated as its child. Continuation
135	indentation inside expressions is balanced independently and cannot terminate
136	the surrounding namespace scope.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## Using Directives
141	
142	Using directives retain their complete C# meaning. Exact duplicates are removed
143	using the full `(target, alias, static, global, namespace scope)` tuple;
144	directives that share a target but differ in alias, flags, or scope remain
145	distinct. Directives inside `§NS` are emitted inside that C# namespace scope;
146	global and compilation-unit usings remain outside all namespace declarations.
147	
148	```calor
149	§U{System.Collections.Generic}             // using System.Collections.Generic;
150	§U{Gen:System.Collections.Generic}         // using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
151	§U{static:System.Math}                     // using static System.Math;
152	§U{global:System.Text}                     // global using System.Text;
153	§U{global:Gen:System.Collections.Generic}  // global using Gen = System.Collections.Generic;
154	§U{global:static:System.Math}               // global using static System.Math;
155	```
156	
157	Generated C# is standalone: namespace dependencies are registered from AST
158	nodes and type references, and compilation does not require SDK implicit
159	usings.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## Functions
164	
165	Functions are the primary code containers.
166	
167	### Syntax
168	
169	```
170	§F{name:visibility}
171	  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
172	  §O{type}             // output (required)
173	  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
174	  §Q condition         // preconditions (0 or more)
175	  §S condition         // postconditions (0 or more)
176	  // body
177	```
178	
179	### Visibility
180	
181	| Value | Meaning | C# Equivalent |
182	|:------|:--------|:--------------|
183	| `pub` | Public | `public static` |
184	| `pri` | Private to the Calor module | `private static` |
185	
186	Namespace scopes do not create separate Calor modules. A module function,
187	including a private function, is callable from every `§NS` scope in the same
188	`ModuleNode`; overload resolution still uses the declared signatures. Because
189	those scopes emit as separate C# static classes, the compiler qualifies sibling
190	calls and may widen the generated member to `internal` as an implementation
191	detail. Private functions are never exported to another input file's
192	cross-module call map.
193	
194	### Examples
195	
196	**Simple function:**
197	```
198	§F{Add:pub}
199	  §I{i32:a}
200	  §I{i32:b}
201	  §O{i32}
202	  §R (+ a b)
203	```
204	
205	**Function with effects:**
206	```
207	§F{PrintSum:pub}
208	  §I{i32:a}
209	  §I{i32:b}
210	  §O{void}
211	  §E{cw}
212	  §P (+ a b)
213	```
214	
215	**Function with contracts:**
216	```
217	§F{Divide:pub}
218	  §I{i32:a}
219	  §I{i32:b}
220	  §O{i32}
221	  §Q (!= b 0)
222	  §R (/ a b)
223	```
224	
225	---
226	
227	## Async Functions
228	
229	Async functions use `§AF` instead of `§F` and automatically wrap return types in `Task<T>`.
230	
231	### Syntax
232	
233	```
234	§AF{name:visibility}
235	  §I{type:param}       // inputs (0 or more)
236	  §O{type}             // output (auto-wrapped to Task<T>)
237	  // body with §AWAIT expressions
238	```
239	
240	### Examples
241	
242	**Simple async function:**
243	```
244	§AF{FetchDataAsync:pub}
245	  §I{str:url}
246	  §O{str}
247	  §B{result} §AWAIT §C{httpClient.GetStringAsync} §A url §/C
248	  §R result
249	```
250	
251	Emits C#:
252	```csharp
253	public static async Task<string> FetchDataAsync(string url)
254	{
255	    var result = await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url);
256	    return result;
257	}
258	```
259	
260	**Async void function (returns Task):**
261	```
262	§AF{ProcessAsync:pub}
263	  §O{void}
264	  §AWAIT §C{Task.Delay} §A 1000 §/C
265	```
266	
267	### Automatic Task Wrapping
268	
269	| Declared Output | Emitted Return Type |
270	|:----------------|:--------------------|
271	| `§O{void}` | `Task` |
272	| `§O{i32}` | `Task<int>` |
273	| `§O{str}` | `Task<string>` |
274	| `§O{Task<i32>}` | `Task<int>` (no double-wrap) |
275	
276	---
277	
278	## Async Methods
279	
280	Async methods in classes use `§AMT` instead of `§MT`.
281	
282	### Syntax
283	
284	```
285	§AMT{id:name:visibility}
286	  §I{type:param}
287	  §O{type}
288	  // body
289	```
290	
291	### Example
292	
293	```
294	§CL{c001:DataService:pub}
295	  §AMT{mt001:GetUserAsync:pub}
296	    §I{i32:id}
297	    §O{User}
298	    §B{user} §AWAIT §C{_repository.FindAsync} §A id §/C
299	    §R user
300	```
301	
302	### Modifiers
303	
304	Async methods support the same modifiers as regular methods:
305	
306	```
307	§AMT{mt001:ProcessAsync:pub:virt}    // public virtual async
308	§AMT{mt002:HandleAsync:prot:ovr}     // protected override async
309	§AMT{mt003:ComputeAsync:pub:stat}    // public static async
310	```
311	
312	---
313	
314	## Await Expression
315	
316	Use `§AWAIT` to await async operations.
317	
318	### Syntax
319	
320	```
321	§AWAIT expression                    // Simple await
322	§AWAIT{false} expression             // await with ConfigureAwait(false)
323	§AWAIT{true} expression              // await with ConfigureAwait(true)
324	```
325	
326	### Examples
327	
328	**Simple await:**
329	```
330	§B{data} §AWAIT §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
331	```
332	
333	**With ConfigureAwait(false) for library code:**
334	```
335	§B{data} §AWAIT{false} §C{client.GetAsync} §A url §/C
336	```
337	
338	Emits: `var data = await client.GetAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false);`
339	
340	### Using Await in Conditions and Expressions
341	
342	```
343	§IF{if1} §AWAIT §C{IsValidAsync} §A id §/C
344	  §P "Valid"
345	
346	§R §AWAIT §C{ComputeAsync} §A x §/C
347	```
348	
349	---
350	
351	## Lambda Expressions
352	
353	Lambda expressions create anonymous functions using `§LAM`/`§/LAM` blocks.
354	
355	### Syntax
356	
357	```
358	§LAM{id:param1:type1}              // single parameter
359	§LAM{id:param1:type1:param2:type2} // multiple parameters
360	§LAM{id}                           // no parameters
361	```
362	
363	The header encodes parameters as colon-separated `name:type` pairs after the ID.
364	Parameters without known types use `object` as the default type.
365	
366	### Single Parameter
367	
368	```
369	§B{doubler} §LAM{lam1:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam1}
370	```
371	
372	Emits: `var doubler = (int x) => x * 2;`
373	
374	### Multiple Parameters
375	
376	Parameters are listed as consecutive `name:type` pairs:
377	
378	```
379	§B{add} §LAM{lam1:a:i32:b:i32} (+ a b) §/LAM{lam1}
380	```
381	
382	Emits: `var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;`
383	
384	**Three parameters:**
385	```
386	§B{combine} §LAM{lam1:x:i32:y:str:z:bool} §C{Process} §A x §A y §A z §/C §/LAM{lam1}
387	```
388	
389	### No Parameters
390	
391	```
392	§B{getTime} §LAM{lam1} §C{DateTime.Now} §/C §/LAM{lam1}
393	```
394	
395	### As LINQ Arguments
396	
397	Lambdas are commonly used as arguments inside `§C{...}` calls:
398	
399	```
400	§C{numbers.Where} §A §LAM{lam1:n:i32} (!= (% n 3) 0) §/LAM{lam1} §/C
401	§C{items.Select} §A §LAM{lam2:x:i32} (* x 2) §/LAM{lam2} §/C
402	```
403	
404	### Statement Body Lambdas
405	
406	For multi-statement bodies, include statements between the tags:
407	
408	```
409	§B{printer} §LAM{lam1:x:i32}
410	§P x
411	§P (* x 2)
412	§/LAM{lam1}
413	```
414	
415	### Async Lambdas
416	
417	Add `async` after the ID, before parameters:
418	
419	```
420	§LAM{lam1:async:x:i32}
421	§B{result} §AWAIT §C{ProcessAsync} §A x §/C
422	§R result
423	§/LAM{lam1}
424	```
425	
426	> **Note:** `§I{type:name}` inline parameter declarations are NOT supported inside
427	> `§LAM` headers. All parameters must be encoded in the header using the
428	> `name:type` pair format.
429	
430	---
431	
432	## Delegate Definitions
433	
434	Delegates define function signatures that can be passed as values.
435	
436	### Syntax
437	
438	```
439	§DEL{id:name}
440	  §I{type:param}       // parameters (0 or more)
441	  §O{type}             // return type (optional for void)
442	  §E{effects}          // effects (optional)
443	```
444	
445	### Examples
446	
447	**Calculator delegate:**
448	```
449	§DEL{d001:Calculator}
450	  §I{i32:a}
451	  §I{i32:b}
452	  §O{i32}
453	```
454	
455	Emits: `public delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);`
456	
457	**Void delegate:**
458	```
459	§DEL{d001:Logger}
460	  §I{str:message}
461	```
462	
463	Emits: `public delegate void Logger(string message);`
464	
465	**Delegate with effects:**
466	```
467	§DEL{d001:FileProcessor}
468	  §I{str:path}
469	  §O{bool}
470	  §E{fs:rw}
471	```
472	
473	---
474	
475	## Enum Definitions
476	
477	Enums define a set of named constants.
478	
479	### Syntax
480	
481	```
482	§EN{id:Name}
483	  Member1
484	  Member2 = 1
485	  Member3 = 2
486	```
487	
488	With underlying type:
489	```
490	§EN{id:Name:underlyingType}
491	  ...
492	```
493	
494	### Examples
495	
496	**Simple enum:**
497	```
498	§EN{e001:Color}
499	  Red
500	  Green
501	  Blue
502	```
503	
504	Emits:
505	```csharp
506	public enum Color
507	{
508	    Red,
509	    Green,
510	    Blue,
511	}
512	```
513	
514	**Enum with explicit values:**
515	```
516	§EN{e001:StatusCode}
517	  Ok = 200
518	  NotFound = 404
519	  Error = 500
520	```
521	
522	**Enum with underlying type:**
523	```
524	§EN{e001:Flags:u8}
525	  None = 0
526	  Read = 1
527	  Write = 2
528	```
529	
530	Emits:
531	```csharp
532	public enum Flags : byte
533	{
534	    None = 0,
535	    Read = 1,
536	    Write = 2,
537	}
538	```
539	
540	---
541	
542	## Enum Extension Methods
543	
544	Extension methods can be added to enums using `§EEXT` (Enum EXTension).
545	
546	### Syntax
547	
548	```
549	§EEXT{id:EnumName}
550	  §F{f001:MethodName:pub}
551	    §I{EnumName:self}
552	    §O{returnType}
553	    // body using self
554	```
555	
556	The first parameter with the enum type (or named `self`) becomes the `this` parameter.
557	
558	### Example
559	
560	```
561	§EN{e001:Color}
562	  Red
563	  Green
564	  Blue
565	
566	§EEXT{ext001:Color}
567	  §F{f001:ToHex:pub}
568	    §I{Color:self}
569	    §O{str}
570	    §W{sw1} self
571	    §K Color.Red → §R "#FF0000"
572	    §K Color.Green → §R "#00FF00"
573	    §K Color.Blue → §R "#0000FF"
574	
575	  §F{f002:IsPrimary:pub}
576	    §I{Color:self}
577	    §O{bool}
578	    §R (|| (== self Color.Red) (|| (== self Color.Green) (== self Color.Blue)))
579	```
580	
581	Emits:
582	```csharp
583	public enum Color
584	{
585	    Red,
586	    Green,
587	    Blue,
588	}
589	
590	public static class ColorExtensions
591	{
592	    public static string ToHex(this Color self)
593	    {
594	        return self switch
595	        {
596	            Color.Red => "#FF0000",
597	            Color.Green => "#00FF00",
598	            Color.Blue => "#0000FF",
599	            _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(self))
600	        };
601	    }
602	
603	    public static bool IsPrimary(this Color self)
604	    {
605	        return self == Color.Red || self == Color.Green || self == Color.Blue;
606	    }
607	}
608	```
609	
610	---
611	
612	## Event Definitions
613	
614	Events allow objects to notify subscribers of state changes.
615	
616	### Syntax
617	
618	```
619	§EVT{id:name:visibility:delegateType}
620	```
621	
622	| Part | Description |
623	|:-----|:------------|
624	| `id` | Unique identifier |
625	| `name` | Event name |
626	| `visibility` | `pub`, `pri`, `prot` |
627	| `delegateType` | Delegate type for handlers |
628	
629	### Example
630	
631	```
632	§CL{c001:Button:pub}
633	  §EVT{e001:Click:pub:EventHandler}
634	    §EVT{e002:ValueChanged:pub:EventHandler<ValueChangedEventArgs>}
635	```
636	
637	Emits:
638	```csharp
639	public class Button
640	{
641	    public event EventHandler Click;
642	    public event EventHandler<ValueChangedEventArgs> ValueChanged;
643	}
644	```
645	
646	---
647	
648	## Event Subscribe/Unsubscribe
649	
650	Use `§SUB` and `§UNSUB` to add or remove event handlers.
651	
652	### Syntax
653	
654	```
655	§SUB eventRef handlerRef      // Subscribe
656	§UNSUB eventRef handlerRef    // Unsubscribe
657	```
658	
659	### Examples
660	
661	**Subscribe to event:**
662	```
663	§SUB button.Click OnButtonClick
664	```
665	
666	Emits: `button.Click += OnButtonClick;`
667	
668	**Unsubscribe from event:**
669	```
670	§UNSUB button.Click OnButtonClick
671	```
672	
673	Emits: `button.Click -= OnButtonClick;`
674	
675	**Subscribe with lambda:**
676	```
677	§SUB button.Click (sender, e) → §P "Clicked!"
678	```
679	
680	---
681	
682	## Input Parameters
683	
684	Input parameters define function arguments.
685	
686	### Syntax
687	
688	```
689	§I{type:name}
690	```
691	
692	### Examples
693	
694	```
695	§I{i32:x}           // int x
696	§I{str:name}        // string name
697	§I{bool:flag}       // bool flag
698	§I{?i32:maybeVal}   // int? maybeVal (nullable)
699	§I{[u8}:data}       // byte[] data
700	§I{[str}:args}      // string[] args
701	```
702	
703	### Multiple Parameters
704	
705	```
706	§F{f001:Add:pub}
707	  §I{i32:a}
708	  §I{i32:b}
709	  §I{i32:c}
710	  §O{i32}
711	  §R (+ (+ a b) c)
712	```
713	
714	---
715	
716	## Output Type
717	
718	Every function must declare its output type.
719	
720	### Syntax
721	
722	```
723	§O{type}
724	```
725	
726	### Examples
727	
728	```
729	§O{void}     // returns nothing
730	§O{i32}      // returns int
731	§O{str}      // returns string
732	§O{?i32}     // returns nullable int
733	§O{i32!str}  // returns Result<int, string>
734	§O{[u8}}     // returns byte[]
735	§O{[str}}    // returns string[]
736	```
737	
738	---
739	
740	## Array Types
741	
742	Calor uses bracket notation `[T]` for array types, which aligns with common programming language conventions.
743	
744	### Syntax
745	
746	```
747	[elementType]         // Single-dimensional array
748	[[elementType]]       // Jagged array (array of arrays)
749	```
750	
751	### Examples
752	
753	| Calor Type | C# Equivalent |
754	|:----------|:--------------|
755	| `[u8]` | `byte[]` |
756	| `[i32]` | `int[]` |
757	| `[str]` | `string[]` |
758	| `[bool]` | `bool[]` |
759	| `[[i32]]` | `int[][]` |
760	
761	### Usage in Fields and Methods
762	
763	```
764	§CL{c001:DataProcessor}
765	  §FLD{[u8}:_buffer:priv}       // private byte[] _buffer
766	  §FLD{[i32}:_indices:priv}     // private int[] _indices
767	
768	  §MT{m001:ProcessData:pub}
769	    §I{[str}:args}              // string[] args parameter
770	    §O{i32}
771	    §R args.Length
772	```
773	
774	---
775	
776	## Block Structure (Indentation)
777	
778	Calor blocks are delimited by **indentation**, like Python. A block
779	opens with one of the structural tags (`§M`, `§F`, `§AF`, `§MT`,
780	`§AMT`, `§CL`, `§IFACE`, `§L`, `§WH`, `§DO`, `§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`,
781	`§LAM`, `§DEL`, `§EN`, `§EEXT`, `§PROP`) and ends at the next line that
782	dedents back to (or past) the parent column.
783	
784	### Rules
785	
786	1. The compiler default is **2 spaces per nesting level**
787	2. Tabs and spaces must not be mixed within a block
788	3. Chain continuations (`§EI`, `§EL`, `§K`, `§WHEN`, `§CA`, `§FI`)
789	   sit at the **same** column as their parent (`§IF`, `§W`, `§TR`),
790	   not indented inside it <!-- drift:ignore -->
791	4. Closer tags were removed in Phase 4d — an explicit `§/X` raises `Calor0830`
792	
793	### Example
794	
795	```
796	§M{m1:Example}
797	  §F{f1:Main:pub} () -> void
798	    §E{cw}
799	    §L{l1:i:1:10:1}
800	      §IF{if1} (> i 5)
801	        §P i
802	      §EL
803	        §P "small"
804	```
805	
806	Each block above (`§IF`, `§L`, `§F`, `§M`) ends purely at its dedent —
807	there are no closer tags. Writing an explicit `§/I`, `§/L`, `§/F`, or
808	`§/M` now raises `Calor0830`.
809	
810	### Tag Reference
811	
812	| Opener | Purpose |
813	|:-------|:--------|
814	| `§M{name}` | Module |
815	| `§F{name:vis}` | Function |
816	| `§AF{name:vis}` | Async function |
817	| `§CL{name}` | Class |
818	| `§IFACE{name}` | Interface |
819	| `§MT{name:vis}` | Method |
820	| `§AMT{name:vis}` | Async method |
821	| `§L{var:from:to:step}` | For loop |
822	| `§WH cond` | While loop |
823	| `§DO` | Do-while loop (condition on closing line during transition) |
824	| `§IF cond` | Conditional (with `§EI` / `§EL` continuations) |
825	| `§W expr` | Switch (with `§K` cases) |
826	| `§TR` | Try (with `§CA` / `§FI`) |
827	| `§LAM{params}` | Lambda (block body) |
828	| `§DEL{name}` | Delegate definition |
829	| `§EN{name}` | Enum |
830	| `§EEXT{enumName}` | Enum extension methods |
831	| `§PROP{name:type:vis}` | Property |
832	| `§EVT{name:vis:type}` | Event (single line, no block) |
833	| `§C{target}` | Call expression (`§/C` ends the argument list) |
834	
835	---
836	
837	## Generics
838	
839	Calor supports generic functions, classes, interfaces, and methods using angle bracket syntax.
840	
841	### Type Parameters
842	
843	Type parameters are declared using `<T>` suffix syntax after the tag attributes.
844	
845	```
846	§F{id:name:vis}<T>         // Generic function with one type parameter
847	§F{id:name:vis}<T, U>      // Generic function with two type parameters
848	§CL{id:name}<T>            // Generic class
849	§IFACE{id:name}<T>         // Generic interface
850	§MT{id:name:vis}<T>        // Generic method
851	```
852	
853	Variance is legal only on interface type parameters:
854	
855	```calor
856	§IFACE{i001:IProducer}<out T>
857	§IFACE{i002:IConsumer}<in T>
858	```
859	
860	Using `in` or `out` on a class, function, or method type parameter is a
861	`Calor0119` error.
862	
863	### Constraints
864	
865	Type parameter constraints are declared using `§WHERE` clauses.
866	
867	**New syntax (recommended):**
868	```
869	§WHERE T : class                    // T must be a reference type
870	§WHERE T : class?                   // T may be a nullable reference type
871	§WHERE T : struct                   // T must be a value type
872	§WHERE T : unmanaged                // T must be unmanaged
873	§WHERE T : notnull                  // T must be non-null
874	§WHERE T : new()                    // T must have parameterless constructor
875	§WHERE T : IComparable<T>           // T must implement interface
876	§WHERE T : class, IComparable<T>    // Multiple constraints
877	§WHERE T : default                  // Override or explicit-interface method only
878	§WHERE T : allows ref struct        // Ref-struct anti-constraint
879	```
880	
881	Using `default` on an interface/class type parameter, interface method,
882	ordinary class method, or module function is a `Calor0120` error. It is
883	preserved only on C#-legal override methods and explicit interface
884	implementations.
885	
886	**Legacy syntax (still supported):**
887	```
888	§WR{T:class}                        // T must be a reference type
889	§WR{T:IComparable}                  // T must implement interface
890	```
891	
892	### Generic Type References
893	
894	Generic types are written inline using angle bracket syntax.
895	
896	```
897	§I{List<T>:items}                   // Parameter of type List<T>
898	§I{Dictionary<str, T>:lookup}       // Nested generic types
899	§O{IEnumerable<T>}                  // Generic return type
900	§FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}            // Generic field type
901	```
902	
903	### Examples
904	
905	**Generic identity function:**
906	```
907	§F{f001:Identity:pub}<T>
908	  §I{T:value}
909	  §O{T}
910	  §R value
911	```
912	
913	**Generic class with constraint:**
914	```
915	§CL{c001:Repository:pub}<T>
916	  §WHERE T : class
917	  §FLD{List<T>:_items:pri}
918	
919	  §MT{m001:Add:pub}
920	    §I{T:item}
921	    §O{void}
922	    §C{_items.Add} §A item §/C
923	
924	  §MT{m002:GetAll:pub}
925	    §O{IReadOnlyList<T>}
926	    §R _items
927	```
928	
929	**Generic interface:**
930	```
931	§IFACE{i001:IRepository}<T>
932	  §WHERE T : class
933	  §MT{m001:Get}
934	    §I{i32:id}
935	    §O{T}
936	```
937	
938	---
939	
940	## C# Attributes
941	
942	C# attributes are preserved during conversion using inline bracket syntax `[@Attribute]`.
943	
944	### Syntax
945	
946	```
947	§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName]
948	§CL{id:name}[@AttributeName(args)]
949	§MT{id:name:vis}[@Attr1][@Attr2]
950	```
951	
952	### Examples
953	
954	**Class with routing attributes (ASP.NET Core):**
955	```
956	§CL{c001:JoinController:ControllerBase}[@Route("api/[controller]")][@ApiController]
957	  §MT{m001:Post:pub}[@HttpPost]
958	```
959	
960	**Property with validation:**
961	```
962	§PROP{p001:Email:str:pub}[@Required][@EmailAddress]
963	  §GET
964	    §SET
965	```
966	
967	### Attribute Arguments
968	
969	| Style | Syntax | Example |
970	|:------|:-------|:--------|
971	| No args | `[@Name]` | `[@ApiController]` |
972	| Positional | `[@Name(value)]` | `[@Route("api/test")]` |
973	| Named | `[@Name(Key="value")]` | `[@JsonProperty(PropertyName="id")]` |
974	| Mixed | `[@Name(pos, Key=val)]` | `[@Range(1, 100, ErrorMessage="Invalid")]` |
975	
976	### Supported Elements
977	
978	Attributes can be attached to:
979	- Classes: `§CL{...}[@attr]`
980	- Interfaces: `§IFACE{...}[@attr]`
981	- Methods: `§MT{...}[@attr]`
982	- Properties: `§PROP{...}[@attr]`
983	- Fields: `§FLD{...}[@attr]`
984	- Parameters: `§I{type:name}[@attr]`
985	
986	---
987	
988	## Why Indent-Based Blocks?
989	
990	1. **Familiar to agents** - LLMs trained on Python have strong priors for indentation <!-- drift:ignore -->
991	2. **Tag-light** - No `§/X` to type, no mismatched-closer errors
992	3. **Refactoring safe** - Stable IDs on openers still survive code movement
993	4. **Lower edit cost** - In edit-workload studies, indent form reduced agent token cost by ~16% with no regression in correctness
994	
995	---
996	
997	## Next
998	
999	- [Types](/calor/syntax-reference/types/) - Type system reference
1000
